title: Fluova Practice Test 2
notes: Second spec-faithful test, assembled from the question bank (all units new). Explanations are available in English and Turkish.

intro.en: Reading: Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life and Read an Academic Passage. After the first module the section adapts to you and gets harder or easier. Correct answers often do not repeat the words in the text; they say the same thing in other words.
intro.tr: Reading: Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life ve Read an Academic Passage. İlk modülden sonra bölüm sana göre zorlaşır ya da kolaylaşır. Doğru cevaplar çoğu zaman metindeki kelimeleri tekrar etmez; anlamı başka sözcüklerle verir.
intro.es: Reading: Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life y Read an Academic Passage. Después del primer módulo, la sección se adapta a ti y se vuelve más difícil o más fácil. Las respuestas correctas a menudo no repiten las palabras del texto: dicen lo mismo con otras palabras.

screens.title: Complete the Words: Flat maps
text: Every flat map of the world contains some distortion. The {{ctw_flat_maps_1}} of a {{ctw_flat_maps_2}} is {{ctw_flat_maps_3}}, and {{ctw_flat_maps_4}} cannot {{ctw_flat_maps_5}} spread {{ctw_flat_maps_6}} paper {{ctw_flat_maps_7}} stretching {{ctw_flat_maps_8}} tearing. {{ctw_flat_maps_9}} must {{ctw_flat_maps_10}} decide which features to keep accurate. One popular design keeps the shapes of coastlines correct but greatly enlarges regions near the poles. As a result, Greenland appears almost as large as Africa, although Africa is about fourteen times bigger.

screens.title: Complete the Words: Desert plants
text: Many desert plants survive long periods without rain. Their {{ctw_desert_plants_1}} spread {{ctw_desert_plants_2}} just {{ctw_desert_plants_3}} the {{ctw_desert_plants_4}}, so {{ctw_desert_plants_5}} can {{ctw_desert_plants_6}} water {{ctw_desert_plants_7}} after a {{ctw_desert_plants_8}} storm. {{ctw_desert_plants_9}} species {{ctw_desert_plants_10}} this water in thick stems or leaves that swell like sponges. A waxy coating on the surface reduces the amount of moisture that escapes into the dry air. Other plants avoid the hottest months entirely by remaining as seeds in the soil until conditions improve.

screens.title: Print Center: New Printing Credits
text: Campus Print Center — New Printing Credits

Starting March 1, every student will receive 200 free printing credits per semester on their student ID card. One black-and-white page uses one credit, and a color page uses five. Unused credits do not carry over to the next semester. Additional credits can be purchased at the front desk or online through the student portal.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To explain a new way students will pay for printing
To announce that the print center will close in March
To remind students to renew their ID cards
To advertise a sale on color printers

why.en: Main purpose (paraphrase): a new credit system for printing. C and D reuse words from the notice (ID card, color) with a different meaning.
why.tr: Ana amaç (parafraz): baskı için yeni kredi sistemi. C ve D metindeki kelimeleri (ID card, color) farklı anlamda kullanıyor.
why.es: Propósito principal (paráfrasis): un nuevo sistema de créditos para imprimir. C y D reutilizan palabras del aviso (ID card, color) con otro significado.

questions.stem: What is true about credits that are not used?
options: They can be exchanged for cash at the front desk
They expire at the end of each term
They are added to the next semester's total
They can be used only for color pages

why.en: Paraphrase: "do not carry over to the next semester" = they expire. C says the opposite; A borrows "front desk".
why.tr: Parafraz: "do not carry over" = dönem sonunda geçersiz olur. C tam tersini söylüyor; A "front desk" ifadesini ödünç alıyor.
why.es: Paráfrasis: "do not carry over to the next semester" = caducan. C dice lo contrario; A toma prestado "front desk".

screens.title: Building email: water shut-off
text:
From: Daniel Reyes (Apartment 4B)
To: All residents
Subject: Water shut-off on Thursday

Hi everyone, the building manager asked me to pass this on. Workers will replace the main water pipe on Thursday, so the water will be turned off from 9 a.m. to about 3 p.m. Please fill a few bottles the night before if you need water for cooking. The laundry room will also be closed that day, but it will reopen on Friday morning with two new washing machines. If you have questions, please contact the office directly rather than replying to this email.
— Daniel

questions.stem: Why did Daniel write the email?
options: To ask the manager to repair a pipe in his apartment
To invite residents to try the new washing machines
To warn neighbors about a planned interruption in service
To complain about the noise from the construction work next door

why.en: Purpose (paraphrase): the water will be turned off for repairs. A misreads who is asking for the repair; B picks a minor detail.
why.tr: Amaç (parafraz): onarım için suyun kesileceği uyarısı. A onarımı kimin istediğini yanlış okuyor; B küçük bir ayrıntıyı ana amaç sanıyor.
why.es: Propósito (paráfrasis): se cortará el agua por unas reparaciones. A malinterpreta quién pide la reparación; B se queda con un detalle menor.

questions.stem: What are residents advised to do?
options: Do their laundry early on Thursday morning
Send any questions to Daniel by email
Avoid cooking until the pipe is replaced
Store some water before the work begins

why.en: Paraphrase of "fill a few bottles the night before". B contradicts the email (contact the office, not Daniel); A is impossible because the laundry room is closed.
why.tr: "Fill a few bottles the night before" ifadesinin parafrazı. B e-postayla çelişiyor (Daniel'e değil ofise yazılmalı); A imkânsız çünkü çamaşırhane kapalı.
why.es: Paráfrasis de "fill a few bottles the night before". B contradice el correo (hay que contactar con la oficina, no con Daniel); A es imposible porque la lavandería está cerrada.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the laundry room?
options: It will be closed for the rest of the week
Its equipment is being upgraded
It is the reason the water must be turned off
It will be open only to residents of Apartment 4B

why.en: Inference: it "will reopen ... with two new washing machines". A contradicts "reopen on Friday"; C confuses the cause of the shut-off.
why.tr: Çıkarım: "iki yeni çamaşır makinesiyle yeniden açılacak". A "Cuma açılacak" bilgisiyle çelişiyor; C kesintinin nedenini karıştırıyor.
why.es: Inferencia: "will reopen ... with two new washing machines". A contradice "reopen on Friday"; C confunde la causa del corte.

screens.title: The Invention of Standard Time
text: Until the late nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, so the time in one city could differ by several minutes from the time in a city a short distance to the east or west.

This local system caused few problems while travel was slow. The arrival of railroads, however, changed the situation. Each railway company kept its own schedule, and a single station might display several clocks showing different times. Passengers often missed connections.

In 1883, railroads in the United States and Canada adopted a system of time zones, each differing from its neighbor by exactly one hour. Many communities at first resisted giving up "sun time," but the convenience of the new system gradually won acceptance.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why railroad companies charged different prices
Why people preferred sun time to railroad time
How faster travel led to a shared way of keeping time
How engineers built more accurate clocks

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). B reverses the outcome; A and D are not discussed.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). B sonucu tersine çeviriyor; A ve D metinde yok.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis). B invierte el resultado; A y D no se tratan.

questions.stem: The word "adopted" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: officially ended
carefully tested
strongly opposed
began to use

why.en: Vocabulary in context: adopted a system = began to use it.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: adopted a system = kullanmaya başladı.
why.es: Vocabulario en contexto: adopted a system = empezó a usarlo.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that a station "might display several clocks showing different times"?
options: To show how confusing travel had become
To describe the design of early railway stations
To explain why clocks were expensive at the time
To argue that railway workers were careless

why.en: Author's purpose: an example of the confusion caused by local time. B takes the example literally.
why.tr: Yazarın amacı: yerel saatin yarattığı karmaşaya örnek. B örneği gerçek anlamıyla alıyor.
why.es: Propósito del autor: un ejemplo de la confusión que causaba la hora local. B toma el ejemplo de forma literal.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the time before railroads?
options: Most travelers carried several clocks with them
Slight differences between places mattered little
Towns to the east always set their clocks a little later
Governments required every town to use sun time

why.en: Inference from "caused few problems while travel was slow". C reverses the direction; D is not stated.
why.tr: "Yolculuk yavaşken pek sorun çıkarmadı" ifadesinden çıkarım. C yönü tersine çeviriyor; D metinde yok.
why.es: Inferencia a partir de "caused few problems while travel was slow". C invierte la dirección; D no se dice.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what was true of the new time zones?
options: Each zone still set its clocks by the local sun
They were first used in European cities
Neighboring zones were exactly one hour apart
Communities accepted them immediately

why.en: Detail: "each differing from its neighbor by exactly one hour". D contradicts "at first resisted".
why.tr: Ayrıntı: "her biri komşusundan tam bir saat farklı". D "başta direndiler" bilgisiyle çelişiyor.
why.es: Detalle: "each differing from its neighbor by exactly one hour". D contradice "at first resisted".

hard.title: Complete the Words: Ocean acidity
text: Oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide that human activity releases into the atmosphere. When {{ctw_ocean_acidity_1}} gas {{ctw_ocean_acidity_2}} in {{ctw_ocean_acidity_3}}, it {{ctw_ocean_acidity_4}} a {{ctw_ocean_acidity_5}} acid {{ctw_ocean_acidity_6}} gradually {{ctw_ocean_acidity_7}} the water's {{ctw_ocean_acidity_8}}. The {{ctw_ocean_acidity_9}} chemical {{ctw_ocean_acidity_10}} reduces the concentration of carbonate ions, which corals, oysters, and many plankton species require to construct their shells and skeletons. Consequently, organisms in more acidic conditions must expend additional energy on calcification, leaving fewer resources for growth and reproduction.

hard.title: Revised Overnight Parking Policy
text: Revised Overnight Parking Policy

Effective next term, overnight parking in Lots C and D will be limited to vehicles displaying a resident permit. Commuter permits will remain valid in these lots between 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. only; vehicles without a resident permit that remain after 10 p.m. may be towed at the owner's expense. Commuters who occasionally need to stay late for laboratory work or rehearsals may request a free one-night pass from Campus Security at least 24 hours in advance. Passes are limited to six per term. Lot E, behind the stadium, will continue to allow overnight parking for all permit holders.

questions.stem: What is the main change described in the notice?
options: Commuters will no longer be allowed to use Lots C and D at all
Overnight parking in two lots will be reserved for residents
Lot E will now close to all vehicles at 10 p.m.
Resident permits will be given out free of charge

why.en: Main change (paraphrase). A is too extreme (commuters can still park there during the day); C contradicts the last sentence.
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz). A aşırı genelleme (gündüz hâlâ park edebilirler); C son cümleyle çelişiyor.
why.es: Cambio principal (paráfrasis). A es demasiado extremo (los que vienen en coche pueden seguir aparcando allí de día); C contradice la última frase.

questions.stem: What should a commuter with a late rehearsal next term most likely do?
options: Buy a resident permit from the office near the stadium
Request a pass from Campus Security on the night itself
Ask Campus Security for a pass at least a day earlier
Park in Lot C and move the car before 7 a.m.

why.en: Inference: passes must be requested 24 hours in advance. B is the timing trap; D ignores the 10 p.m. limit for commuter permits.
why.tr: Çıkarım: geçiş izni 24 saat önceden istenmeli. B zamanlama tuzağı; D yolcu izinleri için 22.00 sınırını yok sayıyor.
why.es: Inferencia: los pases deben pedirse con 24 horas de antelación. B es la trampa de la hora; D ignora el límite de las 10 p. m. para los permisos de commuter.

questions.stem: What is true about Lot E?
options: It is now reserved for students who live on campus
Its users must leave by 10 p.m. on weekdays
Drivers need a one-night pass to park there
Drivers with any type of permit can stay there all night

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of "continue to allow overnight parking for all permit holders"). A and B apply the new Lot C/D rules to the wrong lot.
why.tr: Ayrıntı ("tüm izin sahiplerine gece park" ifadesinin parafrazı). A ve B, C/D otoparklarının yeni kurallarını yanlış otoparka uyguluyor.
why.es: Detalle (paráfrasis de "continue to allow overnight parking for all permit holders"). A y B aplican las nuevas normas de los aparcamientos C/D al aparcamiento equivocado.

hard.title: Underground Fungal Networks
hard.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Beneath most forests lies an extensive web of fungal threads known as mycorrhizal networks. These fungi colonize the roots of trees, supplying them with water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus in exchange for sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis.

Because a single network can connect the roots of many different trees, researchers have proposed that carbon and other resources may travel from one tree to another through these shared connections. Some experiments have reported that seedlings growing in deep shade receive carbon from larger neighbors, which might improve their chances of survival.

Nevertheless, the more dramatic claims, for instance that mature trees deliberately nurture their offspring or warn neighbors of insect attacks, remain contested. Critics note that many field studies were small, that the direction of transfer is difficult to measure, and that fungi may move resources primarily for their own benefit rather than for that of the forest.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How fungi harm the roots of young trees
Evidence about a forest-wide exchange system and its limits
The way trees warn one another of insect attacks
Methods for growing seedlings in deep shade

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase): the networks, what they may do, and doubts about the strongest claims. C treats a contested claim as fact.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz): ağlar, ne yapıyor olabilecekleri ve en iddialı yorumlara dair şüpheler. C tartışmalı bir iddiayı gerçek gibi sunuyor.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis): las redes, lo que podrían hacer y las dudas sobre las afirmaciones más fuertes. C trata una afirmación discutida como un hecho.

questions.stem: The word "contested" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: forgotten
confirmed
disputed
simplified

why.en: Vocabulary in context: contested claims = claims that are disputed.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: contested = tartışmalı, itiraz edilen.
why.es: Vocabulario en contexto: contested claims = afirmaciones que se discuten.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention seedlings growing in deep shade?
options: To prove that mature trees protect their offspring
To show that young trees grow faster without sunlight
To explain why fungi avoid the roots of small trees
To give an example of evidence that resources may move between trees

why.en: Author's purpose: an experimental result supporting transfer. A overstates it — the author says that claim remains contested.
why.tr: Yazarın amacı: kaynak aktarımını destekleyen bir deney sonucu. A abartıyor; yazar bu iddianın tartışmalı olduğunu söylüyor.
why.es: Propósito del autor: un resultado experimental que apoya la transferencia. A lo exagera: el autor dice que esa afirmación sigue en discusión.

questions.stem: What does the author suggest about popular descriptions of trees "caring" for one another?
options: They are supported by most large field studies
They go further than the current evidence allows
They were first proposed by critics of fungal research
They explain why fungi need phosphorus

why.en: Inference: the critics' points (small studies, hard measurement, fungi's own benefit) imply the claims exceed the evidence. A contradicts "many field studies were small".
why.tr: Çıkarım: eleştiriler (küçük çalışmalar, ölçüm zorluğu, mantarların kendi çıkarı) iddiaların kanıtı aştığını gösteriyor. A "çalışmaların çoğu küçüktü" bilgisiyle çelişiyor.
why.es: Inferencia: los puntos de los críticos (estudios pequeños, medición difícil, el propio beneficio de los hongos) implican que las afirmaciones superan las pruebas. A contradice "many field studies were small".

questions.stem: According to the passage, what do trees provide to the fungi?
options: Water absorbed from the soil
Sugars made through photosynthesis
Phosphorus and other minerals
Protection from insect attacks on the roots

why.en: Detail: fungi get "sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis". A and C are what the fungi give the trees — the direction trap.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: mantarlar "ağaçların fotosentezle ürettiği şekerleri" alır. A ve C mantarların ağaçlara verdikleri — yön tuzağı.
why.es: Detalle: los hongos reciben "sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis". A y C son lo que los hongos dan a los árboles: la trampa de la dirección.

easy.title: Complete the Words: Recycled paper
text: Paper can be recycled several times before it is too weak to use. First, {{ctw_recycled_paper_1}} paper {{ctw_recycled_paper_2}} mixed {{ctw_recycled_paper_3}} water {{ctw_recycled_paper_4}} make a {{ctw_recycled_paper_5}} pulp. {{ctw_recycled_paper_6}} then {{ctw_recycled_paper_7}} ink, {{ctw_recycled_paper_8}}, and {{ctw_recycled_paper_9}} pieces {{ctw_recycled_paper_10}} plastic. The clean pulp is pressed flat and dried on large hot rollers. Each time paper is recycled, its fibers become shorter, so new pulp is often added to keep it strong.

easy.title: Lost and Found
text: Lost and Found
Items found in the Student Center are kept at the information desk for 30 days. To claim an item, describe it and show your student ID. Phones and wallets are taken to Campus Security.

questions.stem: Where should a student go to look for a lost wallet?
options: The information desk
The library front desk
The Student Center café
Campus Security

why.en: Detail: phones and wallets go to Campus Security. A is the general rule for other items — the classic trap.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: telefon ve cüzdanlar Campus Security'ye gider. A diğer eşyalar için genel kural — klasik tuzak.
why.es: Detalle: los teléfonos y las carteras van a Campus Security. A es la norma general para los demás objetos: la trampa clásica.

questions.stem: What must students do to get an item back?
options: Wait at least 30 days
Pay a small fee at the desk
Describe it and show an ID
Fill in a form online

why.en: Detail: "describe it and show your student ID". A misuses the 30-day storage period.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: "tarif et ve öğrenci kimliğini göster". A 30 günlük saklama süresini yanlış kullanıyor.
why.es: Detalle: "describe it and show your student ID". A usa mal el plazo de 30 días de almacenamiento.

easy.title: Why Leaves Change Color
easy.directions: Read an Academic Passage — lower module
text: In summer, leaves are green because they contain a large amount of chlorophyll, a substance that helps plants make food from sunlight. Leaves also contain yellow and orange substances, but the strong green color usually hides them.

In autumn, days become shorter and cooler. Trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green color slowly fades. The yellow and orange colors that were there all along become visible. Some trees also produce new red substances in autumn. Bright, sunny days and cool nights often make these red colors stronger.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why leaves show different colors in autumn
How trees store water and food for the winter
Which trees have the brightest red leaves
Why some leaves stay green all year

why.en: Main idea. The other options are not discussed.
why.tr: Ana fikir. Diğer şıklar metinde ele alınmıyor.
why.es: Idea principal. Las demás opciones no se tratan.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why are leaves green in summer?
options: They contain a lot of chlorophyll
They receive more rain in summer
They have no yellow substances
They are younger than autumn leaves

why.en: Detail: green comes from chlorophyll. C contradicts the text: yellow substances are there but hidden.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: yeşil renk klorofilden gelir. C metinle çelişiyor: sarı maddeler vardır ama gizlidir.
why.es: Detalle: el verde viene de la clorofila. C contradice el texto: las sustancias amarillas están ahí, pero ocultas.

questions.stem: The word "fades" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: spreads quickly
becomes darker
becomes weaker
changes shape

why.en: Vocabulary in context: the green color slowly fades = slowly becomes weaker.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: fades = solar, zayıflar.
why.es: Vocabulario en contexto: the green color slowly fades = se va debilitando poco a poco.

questions.stem: Where do the yellow and orange colors of autumn come from?
options: They are made only after the first frost
They are caused by the cool nights
They come from the soil in autumn
They were in the leaves all summer

why.en: Paraphrase of "were there all along". A and C invent a new source; B is said about the red colors only.
why.tr: "Were there all along" ifadesinin parafrazı. A ve C yeni bir kaynak uyduruyor; B yalnızca kırmızı renkler için söyleniyor.
why.es: Paráfrasis de "were there all along". A y C inventan un origen nuevo; B solo se dice de los colores rojos.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a cloudy autumn with warm nights?
options: The red shades might look duller
Leaves would stay green until winter
Trees would produce more chlorophyll
Yellow colors would not appear

why.en: Inference: sunny days and cool nights make red stronger, so the opposite weather likely makes it weaker. D is too strong — yellow appears anyway.
why.tr: Çıkarım: güneşli gün ve serin gece kırmızıyı güçlendirir, tersi hava muhtemelen zayıflatır. D fazla iddialı — sarı her durumda görünür.
why.es: Inferencia: los días soleados y las noches frescas intensifican el rojo, así que el tiempo contrario probablemente lo debilita. D es demasiado fuerte: el amarillo aparece de todos modos.

intro.en: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, conversations, announcements and academic talks. Each recording plays once; you may take notes. Speakers use US, British and Australian accents. After the first module the section adapts to you and gets harder or easier.
intro.tr: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, konuşmalar, duyurular ve akademik konuşmalar. Her ses bir kez çalınır; not alabilirsiniz. Konuşmacılar ABD, İngiliz ve Avustralya aksanlarıyla konuşur. İlk modülden sonra bölüm sana göre zorlaşır ya da kolaylaşır.
intro.es: Listening: Listen and Choose a Response, conversaciones, avisos y clases académicas. Cada grabación se reproduce una vez; puedes tomar notas. Se oyen acentos de EE. UU., Reino Unido y Australia. Después del primer módulo, la sección se adapta a ti y se vuelve más difícil o más fácil.

audio.text: Could you send me the slides from today's lecture?

options: The lecture was really interesting.
Professor Lin gave it in the big hall this morning.
Sure, I'll email them to you tonight.
I slid on the wet floor earlier.

why.en: Request → agreement. D is a sound-alike trap (slides / slid).
why.tr: Rica → kabul. D ses benzerliği tuzağı (slides / slid).
why.es: Petición → aceptación. D es una trampa de sonido parecido (slides / slid).

audio.text: How long does it take to walk to the stadium?

options: Every Saturday during the season.
I'd rather take the bus there.
About fifteen minutes from here.
It holds about ten thousand people.

why.en: "How long" → a length of time. A gives a frequency, the classic trap.
why.tr: "How long" → süre. A sıklık veriyor; klasik tuzak.
why.es: "How long" → una duración. A da una frecuencia, la trampa clásica.

audio.text: Why didn't you come to the club meeting?

options: Yes, I joined the club last year.
I had a dentist appointment.
It was in the student lounge.
We're meeting again next week.

why.en: "Why" → a reason. A answers a "why" question with "Yes".
why.tr: "Why" → sebep. A "neden" sorusuna "Evet" ile cevap veriyor.
why.es: "Why" → un motivo. A responde a un "why" con "Yes".

audio.text: Who's leading the review session tomorrow?

options: In Room 204 at three o'clock.
Yes, I'm going to review my notes.
It should last about an hour and a half.
One of the teaching assistants, I think.

why.en: "Who" → a person. B answers yes/no and repeats "review".
why.tr: "Who" → kişi. B evet/hayır diyor ve "review" kelimesini tekrar ediyor.
why.es: "Who" → una persona. B responde sí/no y repite "review".

audio.text: Do you know if the bookstore is still open?

options: I think it closes at six on Fridays.
No, I already bought all my books.
It's on the second floor of the library.
The books cost more than I expected.

why.en: An indirect but relevant answer about opening hours. C answers "where", D repeats "books".
why.tr: Açılış saatiyle ilgili dolaylı ama ilgili yanıt. C "nerede" sorusuna cevap veriyor, D "books" kelimesini tekrar ediyor.
why.es: Una respuesta indirecta pero pertinente sobre el horario. C responde a "where"; D repite "books".

audio.text: The vending machine took my money but didn't give me anything.

options: You can ask for a refund at the front desk.
I bought a snack from it this morning.
It's next to the stairs on the second floor.
Yes, it takes both coins and cards now.

why.en: Problem → a solution. B repeats the situation; C answers "where"; D answers a yes/no question nobody asked.
why.tr: Sorun → çözüm. B durumu tekrar ediyor; C "nerede" sorusuna cevap veriyor; D sorulmamış bir evet/hayır sorusunu cevaplıyor.
why.es: Problema → una solución. B repite la situación; C responde a "where"; D responde a una pregunta de sí/no que nadie hizo.

audio.text: Which dorm did you end up choosing?

options: I'm still choosing my classes.
Yes, I moved in last weekend.
My roommate is from Chile.
The one closest to the gym.

why.en: "Which" → a choice. A repeats "choosing" with a different object.
why.tr: "Which" → seçim. A "choosing" kelimesini başka bir nesneyle tekrar ediyor.
why.es: "Which" → una elección. A repite "choosing" con otro objeto.

audio.text: Where should I put these chairs after the event?

screens.title: Academic Talk: How bats hunt in the dark
screens.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in a biology class.

audio.text: Today let's look at how bats find their way in complete darkness. Most bats rely on a process called echolocation. A bat produces a series of very high-pitched calls, usually too high for humans to hear, and then listens for the echoes that bounce back from objects around it. By noticing how long each echo takes to return, the bat can judge how far away an object is, and differences between what its two ears hear tell it the direction.

Now, here's what I find remarkable. When a bat is simply flying across open space, it might call around ten times per second. But as it closes in on an insect, the rate rises sharply, to well over a hundred calls per second. Researchers call this final burst the feeding buzz. The faster calls give the bat almost continuous updates about the insect's position, which matters because the insect is moving too.

Some moths, by the way, have evolved a defense. They can hear bat calls, and when they detect one, they suddenly drop or change direction. A few species even produce clicks of their own that seem to interfere with the bat's signal. So this is really an ongoing contest between hunter and prey.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase of echolocation and hunting). B overgeneralizes the moth example.
why.tr: Ana fikir (yankıyla yer bulma ve avlanma). B güve örneğini abartıyor.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis de la ecolocalización y la caza). B generaliza en exceso el ejemplo de las polillas.

options: It stops calling so the insect cannot hear it.

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of "the rate rises sharply"). A reverses what happens.

hard.title: Academic Talk: Managing shared resources
hard.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: In economics there's a well-known idea called the tragedy of the commons. Picture a pasture that everyone in a village may use. Each herder reasons that adding one more cow brings him the full benefit of that cow, while the cost, slightly less grass, is shared by everyone. So each herder adds cows, and eventually the pasture is ruined, even though no one wanted that outcome.

For a long time, economists assumed there were only two solutions: either the government controls the resource, or it's divided into private property. But the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged that view. She studied fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems around the world that communities had managed successfully for centuries without either solution.

What did those communities have in common? Ostrom found that they set clear boundaries around who could use the resource, they made their own rules about how much each person could take, and, this is important, they monitored one another and applied gradually increasing penalties to people who broke the rules. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this work. So the lesson isn't that shared resources are always doomed. It's that the outcome depends on how the users organize themselves.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the lecture?
options: Shared resources can survive when their users organize well.
Governments should control all natural resources.
Private property is the only way to protect a pasture.
Fisheries are harder to manage than forests.

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase of the conclusion). B and C are the views Ostrom challenged.
why.tr: Ana fikir (sonucun parafrazı). B ve C, Ostrom'un karşı çıktığı görüşler.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis de la conclusión). B y C son las ideas que Ostrom cuestionó.

options: The village requires a minimum number of cows.
He gains the full benefit but shares the cost.
The grass grows back faster with more animals.
He expects the government to divide the pasture.

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of the herder's reasoning). C contradicts the outcome described.
why.tr: Ayrıntı (çobanın mantığının parafrazı). C anlatılan sonuçla çelişiyor.
why.es: Detalle (paráfrasis del razonamiento del pastor). C contradice el resultado descrito.

To show where governments succeeded

why.en: Function: evidence for Ostrom's challenge. A reverses their role.

why.es: Función: pruebas para el cuestionamiento de Ostrom. A invierte su papel.

hard.title: Academic Talk: The rise of linear perspective
hard.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an art history class.

audio.text: Let's turn to one of the great technical advances of the Renaissance: linear perspective. Before the fifteenth century, European painters certainly suggested depth. They placed distant figures higher in the picture or made them smaller, but they lacked a consistent system, and different objects in the same painting often seemed to recede at different angles.

In Florence, early in the fifteenth century, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small panel showing the city's baptistery and drilled a hole through it. A viewer looked through the hole from the back while holding a mirror in front of the panel, so the reflected painting could be compared directly with the real building. The two lined up remarkably well.

The principle behind this is that parallel lines moving away from the viewer appear to meet at a single point, which we now call the vanishing point. In the 1430s, Leon Battista Alberti described the method in writing, which allowed it to spread far beyond Brunelleschi's circle. Keep in mind, though, that perspective wasn't only about accuracy. Painters used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye, often toward the most important figure in the scene.

questions.stem: What is the lecture mainly about?
options: How a system for showing depth developed and spread
Why Renaissance painters preferred religious subjects
How architects designed buildings in Florence
Why paintings before 1400 had no sense of depth

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). D is too extreme: earlier painters did suggest depth.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). D aşırı: önceki ressamlar da derinlik gösteriyordu.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis). D es demasiado extremo: los pintores anteriores sí sugerían profundidad.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of the mirror in Brunelleschi's demonstration?
options: To make the small painting look larger
To let viewers compare the painting with the real building
To light the panel from behind
To hide the hole drilled in the panel

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of "compared directly with the real building").
why.tr: Ayrıntı ("gerçek binayla doğrudan karşılaştırılabilsin" parafrazı).
why.es: Detalle (paráfrasis de "compared directly with the real building").

questions.stem: Why does the professor mention Alberti?
options: To describe a criticism of Brunelleschi
To name the artist who painted the baptistery
To explain how the method became widely known
To show that the method was invented in Rome

why.en: Function: his written description "allowed it to spread". B confuses Alberti with Brunelleschi.
why.tr: İşlev: yazılı anlatımı yöntemin "yayılmasını sağladı". B Alberti'yi Brunelleschi ile karıştırıyor.
why.es: Función: su descripción escrita "allowed it to spread". B confunde a Alberti con Brunelleschi.

questions.stem: What point does the professor make at the end of the lecture?
options: Perspective made paintings less accurate.
Important figures were always painted in the very center.
The vanishing point was rarely used after Alberti.
Perspective also helped direct the viewer's attention.

why.en: Inference from "used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye". B overgeneralizes "often".
why.tr: Çıkarım: "kaçış noktasını izleyicinin bakışını yönlendirmek için kullandılar". B "often" ifadesini genelleştiriyor.
why.es: Inferencia a partir de "used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye". B generaliza en exceso "often".

why.es: Petición → aceptación. B repite "borrow".

easy.title: Conversation: Paying at the cafeteria

Yes, cash or a bank card. It only takes a minute.

questions.stem: What is the man's problem?

He cannot pay with cash at the counter.

questions.stem: What will happen on Saturday?
options: The pool will be cleaned.
The gym will be closed.
The gym will open at eight.
A swimming class will start.

why.en: Detail: the gym closes for cleaning. A moves the cleaning to the pool.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: spor salonu temizlik için kapanıyor. A temizliği havuza taşıyor.
why.es: Detalle: el gimnasio cierra por limpieza. A traslada la limpieza a la piscina.

questions.stem: What is true about the swimming pool?
options: It will be open on Saturday.
It will close on Sunday.
It will open at eight a.m.
It will be cleaned this week.

why.en: Detail: "will stay open as usual on Saturday". C belongs to the gym.

why.es: Detalle: "will stay open as usual on Saturday". C corresponde al gimnasio.

easy.title: Academic Talk: How caves form
easy.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.

audio.text: Today I want to explain how most caves form. It starts with rain. As rainwater moves through the soil, it picks up a gas called carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. When this water reaches limestone rock underground, it slowly dissolves the rock. Over thousands of years, small cracks become wide tunnels and large rooms. Later, water that drips from the ceiling leaves behind tiny amounts of mineral. These build up into the long stone shapes that hang down from cave ceilings. Some of them grow less than a centimeter in a hundred years. So a cave is really made by water, a little bit at a time.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How water creates caves
Why caves are dark and cold
How people explore caves
Where the largest caves are

why.en: Main idea. The other options are not discussed.
why.tr: Ana fikir. Diğer şıklar konuşmada yok.
why.es: Idea principal. Las demás opciones no se tratan.

questions.stem: What happens to rainwater as it moves through the soil?
options: It becomes slightly acidic.
It slowly turns into solid stone.
It gets much colder.
It loses its minerals.

why.en: Paraphrase of "picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid".
why.tr: "Karbondioksit alır ve zayıf bir asit olur" ifadesinin parafrazı.
why.es: Paráfrasis de "picks up carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid".

questions.stem: What kind of rock do these caves form in?
options: Sandstone
Granite
Limestone
Clay

why.en: Detail: limestone.
why.tr: Ayrıntı: kireç taşı.
why.es: Detalle: la piedra caliza.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker say "a little bit at a time"?
options: To say that caves are getting smaller
To explain why caves are small
To describe how rain falls
To show that caves form very slowly

why.en: Function: stresses the slow process ("over thousands of years").
why.tr: İşlev: sürecin yavaşlığını vurguluyor ("binlerce yıl boyunca").
why.es: Función: subraya lo lento del proceso ("over thousands of years").

screens.prompt: Write an email to the seller. In your email, do the following: (1) Explain what you ordered and what you received. (2) Describe why the difference matters for your course. (3) Suggest a way to solve the problem.

When the book arrived, it was a different edition from the one shown in the listing, and your instructor has said that students must use the edition in the listing because the page numbers and exercises are different.

wordTarget.en: At least 100 words. State your opinion, support it, and add your own contribution to the discussion.
wordTarget.tr: En az 100 kelime. Görüşünü belirt, destekle ve tartışmaya kendi katkını ekle.

screens.prompt: Your professor is teaching a class on higher education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words.

professor.name: Halvorsen
professor.post: Many universities now require students to complete an internship before they graduate. Supporters say internships teach practical skills that classes cannot. Others argue that a required internship is unfair to students who already work part-time or who cannot afford to accept an unpaid position. Should universities make an internship a graduation requirement? Why or why not?

students.name: Priya
students.post: I think they should. My cousin did an internship at an engineering firm, and she said she learned more about teamwork in three months than in two years of group projects. Employers also expect some experience now, so a requirement protects students from graduating without any.

students.name: Marcus
students.post: I disagree. I already work twenty hours a week to pay my rent, so an unpaid internship would mean losing my job. A requirement sounds fair, but it really helps students whose families can support them. Universities should encourage internships, not force them.

intro.en: Speaking: two tasks. Each task opens with a scenario. In Listen and Repeat the sentences get longer; in the Interview, the interviewer asks four questions on one topic.

intro.es: Speaking: dos tareas. Cada tarea empieza con un escenario. En Listen and Repeat las oraciones se van alargando; en la entrevista, la persona que entrevista hace cuatro preguntas sobre un mismo tema.
